result: Nuclear envelope breakdown (NEBD) in starfish oocytes is mediated by an Arp2/3-nucleated F-actin shell, which destabilizes the NE by segregating pore-dense and pore-free membranes. This mechanism contrasts with microtubule-driven tearing observed in mammalian somatic cells and provides the first mechanistic explanation for the sudden collapse of the NE structure during its breakdown.
evaluation: Claims C1, C15, C16, and C88 are well-supported by multiple lines of evidence including live-cell imaging (Figure 1A), EM data (Figures 5-7), STED microscopy (Figures 3, 5G), and inhibitor experiments (Figures 1E, 3C). The data consistently demonstrate that F-actin assembly is required for NE rupture and that this mechanism differs from the microtubule-driven process in mammalian cells. The conclusion is based on comprehensive structural and functional data.

result: Actin is nucleated by the Arp2/3 complex within the lamina and forms filopodia-like spikes (0.5-2 μm in length, spaced at ~0.1 μm) that extend towards and protrude nuclear membranes. These spikes contain fibrous densities consistent with actin filaments and grow preferentially from the shell base in the lamina towards nuclear membranes.
evaluation: Claims C2, C37, C38, C45, C51, and C67 are strongly supported by STED microscopy showing F-actin spikes with precise measurements (Figure 3D), EM and tomographic data showing membrane protrusions with actin filaments (Figures 5D, E), and ArpC1 localization at the base of the shell (Figure 3E). The morphology and dimensions are consistently observed across multiple imaging modalities.

result: F-actin spikes protrude pore-free nuclear membranes while NPCs accumulate at the base of spikes, remaining attached to the still-intact lamina. The membrane evaginations are largely free of NPCs because NPCs are held back by their attachments to the lamina while membranes are protruded by actin assembly.
evaluation: Claims C3, C40, C46, C47, C49, C50, and C71 are well-supported by EM data showing membrane spikes free of NPCs with NPC-dense regions at their base (Figures 5D, G), STED imaging showing similar patterns (Figure 5G), and quantification of NPC spacing (Figure 6C). The proposed mechanism that NPCs are held back by lamina attachments is a reasonable inference from the structural data.

result: The lamina remains continuous throughout NEBD, gradually coarsening but not undergoing rapid disassembly or F-actin-induced tearing. The NE rupture does not proceed by tearing or rapid disassembly of the lamina.
evaluation: Claims C29, C30, and C31 are supported by immunofluorescence data showing continuous lamina throughout NEBD (Figure 2B) and STED microscopy showing gradual coarsening of the lamin mesh (Figure 2B). This conclusion is consistent with previous observations and contrasts with the microtubule-driven tearing mechanism in somatic cells.

result: NE rupture proceeds by F-actin-driven sorting of NE membranes into pore-dense and pore-free segments. Pore-dense segments invaginate to form nucleoplasmic bodies, while rupture occurs in evaginating pore-free segments. NPC-free membranes are generated by redistribution of NPCs, with pore-to-pore distance decreasing from ~200 nm to ~100 nm in pore-dense regions.
evaluation: Claims C4, C52, C56, C57, C63, and C64 are strongly supported by EM data showing segregation of pore-free and pore-dense segments (Figure 6A), quantification of NPC spacing (Figure 6C), and observation of rupture in pore-free regions (Figure 7A). The conclusion that NPC-free membranes are generated by redistribution is a reasonable inference from the quantitative data showing increased NPC density in some regions and decreased density in others.

result: Nucleoplasmic bodies are dense, round structures (200-500 nm in diameter) that form by invagination of NPC-rich clusters. They often appear in a beads-on-a-string arrangement and are bounded by closely juxtaposed NPCs with intact central ring structures. As NPCs accumulate between pore-free spikes, the membranes in these NPC-rich dimples buckle into the nucleoplasm and invaginate to form nucleoplasmic bodies.
evaluation: Claims C53, C54, C55, C58, C59, and C72 are well-supported by EM data showing nucleoplasmic bodies with precise measurements (Figures 5D, 6B), tomograms confirming NPC structure (Figures 6D, E), and examination of intermediates suggesting the invagination mechanism (Figures 6A, B). The proposed mechanism of formation is a reasonable inference from the structural intermediates observed.

result: The F-actin shell first appears as an equatorial band of foci when the NE is still intact and impermeable to large dextrans. Approximately 30-45 s later, as F-actin foci grow and merge to form a continuous shell, the first breaks appear allowing large dextrans to enter. During this process, spike-like membrane protrusions appear 10-15 s after F-actin foci begin to assemble, and NPCs appear to separate partially from the membrane. Dextran entry occurs 20-30 s after the initial membrane spikes, when membrane reorganization has progressed to an advanced stage.
evaluation: Claims C17-C23 are directly supported by high-resolution live-cell imaging data (Figures 1A-D) showing the temporal sequence of events with precise timing. The observations are consistent across multiple experiments and provide a detailed timeline of the membrane reorganization process.

result: Membrane reorganization during NEBD is dependent on actin assembly. Inhibiting F-actin shell formation by depleting actin monomers or inhibiting Arp2/3 prevents membrane reorganization and the separation of lamina and membranes, though the nucleus still collapses and the NE ruffles due to partial NE disassembly. Without F-actin assembly, large membrane fragments remain intact long after NEBD.
evaluation: Claims C24-C28 and C36 are supported by experimental data using UtrCH-mediated actin depletion (Figure 1E) and CK-666 inhibitor (Figure 3C), which demonstrate that preventing F-actin shell formation blocks membrane reorganization while allowing nuclear collapse. This provides strong functional evidence for the role of actin assembly in membrane reorganization.

result: The lamina co-localizes with F-actin at the base of the shell, while NPCs form a separate layer up to 500 nm above the F-actin shell. Before NE rupture, NPC and lamina stainings overlap at ~50 nm resolution, but at the shell stage, NPC-stained NE fragments 'float' above the intact lamina. The still-intact lamina serves as the scaffold upon which the F-actin shell assembles, while nuclear membranes fragment and separate away from the lamina and F-actin shell.
evaluation: Claims C32-C35 are supported by immunofluorescence data with line profile analysis (Figures 3A, B), STED data showing separation of NPCs from lamina (Figure 3C), and comparison to pre-NEBD state (Figure 3C). The conclusion that lamina serves as a scaffold is a reasonable inference from the co-localization data.

result: The NE is smooth, continuous, and tightly packed with NPCs at regular spacing (~200 nm) in immature oocytes and intact regions. In areas closer to the rupture site, gaps in NPC occupancy appear and increase in number and size, evolving into bumps and membrane spikes that rise ~1 μm above the level of the NE.
evaluation: Claims C41-C44 are directly supported by EM data (Figures 5A-D) with quantification (Figure 6C) and measurements from tomographic data (Figures 5D, E). The observations are consistent with previous work (Lénárt et al., 2003) and provide a detailed spatial progression of NE changes leading to rupture.

result: Membranes are interrupted in areas where segregation of pore-dense and pore-free regions is strongest and NPC invaginations are most dramatic. In these rupture areas, no continuous membrane boundary separates cyto- and nucleoplasm, but nucleoplasmic bodies are abundant. Light microscopy reveals a complex tubular-vesicular network densely labeled by NPC staining.
evaluation: Claims C60-C62 are supported by EM montages showing rupture sites (Figure 7A) and STED microscopy showing tubular-vesicular networks (Figure 7B). The correlation between EM and light microscopy data strengthens the conclusion about the nature of membrane rupture.

result: The stage when 25-kDa dextran fills the nucleus but 160-kDa dextran is excluded identifies the time-window of F-actin shell formation and NE rupture. NE rupture initiates near the equator of the nucleus and spreads as a wave towards the poles.
evaluation: Claims C91 and C92 are supported by correlative light and EM data (Figures 4A-D) and are consistent with established knowledge about NE permeability during NEBD (Lénárt et al., 2003). The spatial arrangement of rupture is directly observed in EM montages and confirmed by live and fixed light microscopy.

result: NPC-free areas pushed out by the F-actin shell may cause crowding of NPCs in juxtaposed regions. Pore-free nuclear membranes separated from the lamina are unstable and rupture, rearranging into an ER-like reticular structure.
evaluation: Claims C48 and C73 are inferred from EM observations and quantification of NPC spacing (Figure 6C) showing increased density in some regions. While the authors acknowledge they cannot estimate 3D membrane areas from 2D sections, the inference is reasonable based on the observed redistribution of NPCs and rupture occurring in pore-free regions (Figure 7A).

result: F-actin foci form within the lamina when cytoplasmic components reach critical concentration due to NPC disassembly. Once triggered, foci grow rapidly due to autocatalytic Arp2/3-mediated nucleation. The asymmetry in filament growth may be explained by force-promoted nucleation of branched meshwork. The morphology is similar to in vitro F-actin networks on micropatterned Arp2/3, suggesting localized Arp2/3 activation within the lamina may be sufficient to explain the F-actin shell morphology.
evaluation: Claims C65, C66, C68, C69, and C70 are largely speculative or based on analogy to in vitro systems (Reymann et al., 2010; Bieling et al., 2016). While C66 is consistent with observed rapid growth (Figure 1A) and C70 is supported by Arp2/3 localization data (Figure 3E), the specific trigger mechanism (C65) and force-based explanation for asymmetry (C68) remain hypothetical. Additional experiments would be needed to directly test these mechanisms.

result: Detaching nuclear membranes from the lamin network leads to NE rupture in various physiological contexts including cancer cells, micronuclei, and migrating cells. In somatic cells, NEBD proceeds by microtubule-mediated tearing of the lamina, but a similar mechanism based on segregation of lamina, NPCs, and membranes may play a critical role in destabilizing the NE. The segregation of nuclear membranes from the lamin network appears to be a general feature of nuclear rupture in dividing mammalian somatic cells and during interphase NE rupture in cancer cells.
evaluation: Claims C74-C78 and C90 are supported by citations to other work (Hatch et al., 2013; Thiam et al., 2016; Davidson and Lammerding, 2014; Denais et al., 2016; Beaudouin et al., 2002; Salina et al., 2002), but the extension of the starfish oocyte mechanism to mammalian somatic cells (C78, C90) is speculative. The authors acknowledge that the precise morphology of NE intermediates in somatic cells at comparable resolution is not known, making this inference uncertain.

result: F-actin assembly may facilitate NE rupture by increasing membrane tension in evaginations or causing extreme membrane curvatures at invagination boundaries. The ESCRT machinery may be involved in membrane rearrangements during NEBD based on similarities in membrane topology to NE repair processes.
evaluation: Claims C79 and C80 are explicitly speculative. While the authors observe membrane topologies similar to those in ESCRT-mediated processes (Denais et al., 2016; Raab et al., 2016; Olmos et al., 2015), no direct evidence for ESCRT involvement or specific mechanisms of membrane rupture is provided. These remain hypotheses requiring future experimental validation.

result: F-actin shells similar to those in starfish oocytes have been observed in several species including sea urchin, Nematostella vectensis, and polychaete worms. F-actin-mediated NE rupture may be widely spread across animal species, and this mechanism is likely to function in many animal species.
evaluation: Claims C81, C82, and C89 are supported by citations showing F-actin shells in multiple species (Burkel et al., 2007; DuBuc et al., 2014; Jacobsohn, 1999). While the detailed characterization is lacking in these other species, the observation of similar structures across diverse taxa provides reasonable support for the inference that this mechanism may be widespread.

result: The clearing of NPCs off the membrane during NEBD appears to be conserved in organisms with partially open mitosis. In Ustilago maydis, microtubules tear the NE by pulling the nucleus through a small opening, and NPCs initiate release of nucleoporins prior to rupture. In Schizosaccharomyces japonicus, the NE is split by stretching the nucleus between poles, and NPCs are redistributed to the poles, freeing naked membranes at regions destined to be broken.
evaluation: Claims C83-C87 are supported by citations to work in U. maydis and Sz. japonicus (Straube et al., 2005; Aoki et al., 2011; Theisen et al., 2008). The observation that NPC clearing occurs before NE rupture in these organisms, despite different rupture mechanisms, supports the authors' conclusion that this may be a conserved feature.

result: Background information on nuclear envelope structure, oocyte nuclear architecture, and established mechanisms of NEBD across species. The NE is composed of inner and outer membranes fused at NPCs, supported by the lamina. Oocytes have large nuclei densely packed with NPCs. NEBD begins with phosphorylation-driven partial permeabilization allowing small molecules to leak while maintaining overall NE structure. In mammalian cells, microtubules tear the NE in a dynein-dependent process.
evaluation: Claims C5-C14 represent established knowledge supported by appropriate citations (Burke and Ellenberg, 2002; Goldberg and Allen, 1995; Hetzer, 2010; Ungricht and Kutay, 2017; Dultz et al., 2008; Mühlhäusser and Kutay, 2007; Terasaki et al., 2001; Lénárt et al., 2003; Martino et al., 2017; Linder et al., 2017; Beaudouin et al., 2002; Salina et al., 2002). These provide necessary context for the current work.
